💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vanessa Bryant, the widow of Los Angeles Lakers legend Kobe Bryant, has denied a report that she is teaming up with two-time Lakers champion Pau Gasol to attempt to purchase the Los Angeles Sparks.
  • "Another rumor out today… I have never had any conversations about being an NBA or WNBA owner.
  • Sports Business Journal reported on Wednesday that Bryant and Gasol were interested in the Sparks, which were put up for sale in October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vanessa Bryant, the widow of Los Angeles Lakers legend Kobe Bryant, has denied a report that she is teaming up with two-time Lakers champion Pau Gasol to attempt to purchase the Los Angeles Sparks.

"Another rumor out today… I have never had any conversations about being an NBA or WNBA owner. If that was true I would announce it. I'm just over here undecided on what seasonal coffee flavor I like and over caffeinated," Bryant wrote on Instagram. "I can only speak for myself. I don't know what anyone else does or does not have going on.".

Sports Business Journal reported on Wednesday that Bryant and Gasol were interested in the Sparks, which were put up for sale in October. Owner Mark Walter, who has been shedding assets amid an FBI and SEC investigation into his wealth management firm, is seeking a record-shattering $700 million for the franchise and its yet-unopened practice facility, according to Bloomberg. The current record for a WNBA team sale is $300 million, which Tilman Fertitta paid for the Connecticut Sun before moving the franchise to Houston to revive the Comets.

Notably, Josh Kushner and Bob Iger, who purchased the Lakers from Walter earlier this year, are reportedly uninterested in the Sparks. Los Angeles Clippers owner Steve Ballmer reportedly considered bidding on the team in 2024, but is right now prohibited for submitting a bid because he is serving a one-year suspension from the NBA over his role in the Aspiration scandal. However, at least one of the groups bidding for the Sparks, a group of investors put together by Swish Partners, would consider moving the team to Ballmer's Intuit Dome.

Recent findings suggest that gasol already has a financial stake in the WNBA, as he invested in the league's 2022 capital raise. Bryant frequently attends Sparks games and has brought WNBA players in to host clinics at the Mamba & Mambacita Sports Foundation. The late Kobe Bryant was a prominent figure in the women's basketball community, especially coaching his late daughter Gianna's AAU team. Gianna hoped to play for the University of Connecticut and presumably the WNBA afterward before tragically dying in the helicopter accident that killed her father and seven others in 2020.

According to recent reports, several former NBA players own or have owned minority stakes in WNBA teams, including Magic Johnson (Sparks), Dwyane Wade (Chicago Sky), Kyle Lowry (Toronto Tempo) and Grant Hill and Chris Webber (the upcoming Detroit expansion team set to begin play in 2029). However, no former NBA player holds the governorship of a WNBA team. Gasol could change that. If we expand to immediate family, Bryant could become the first spouse of a former NBA player to hold a controlling interest in a WNBA team, though at this stage, the exact structure of a possible Bryant-Gasol bid and the other investors who could be involved are not clear.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After Lions star Aidan Hutchinson tore his ACL going airborne while celebrating a sack in Week 10, Giants running back Cam Skattebo mentioned he'd retire his signature backflip celebration.

It proved a very short retirement.

It has been revealed that skattebo delivered the game-clinching first down in the Giants' 23-18 upset win over the Jaguars and celebrated ... with a backflip.

Skattebo first down and a backflip!JAXvsNYG on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/JuwVc6smEv.

Industry observers note that it was a huge win for the Giants, who moved to 6-3-1 to remain two games up on the Cowboys (5-6) in the NFC East. Dallas won earlier Sunday.

It has been revealed that it was also a huge sigh of relief for Skattebo, who had a crucial fumble that contributed to Jacksonville's late rally. Overall, Skattebo finished with 14 carries for 34 yards.

Sources indicate that john Harbaugh had long been against Skattebo's flipping — Skattebo notably failed on a backflip over the offseason, months after his rookie year ended with a serious ankle injury (not suffered on a flip). He was pleased to hear about Skattebo's intention not to backflip earlier in the week.

Sources indicate that "I support his decision, and I hope he scores a lot of touchdowns," Harbaugh remarked. "I hope he gets an opportunity to prove it real soon. That'd be great.".

After Skattebo reneged, Harbaugh didn't exactly look pleased on the sideline.

Cam Skattebo hit a backflip after saying he wasn't going to do it 👀Check out John Harbaugh's reaction on the sidelines 😭 pic.twitter.com/Z1ucuQzvE7.

After the game, though, Skattebo explained that the charged atmosphere and the significance of the first down played huge roles.

Sources indicate that "When energy calls for it, it calls for it," Skattebo noted. "My teammates, I do whatever I can to bring the energy for the team. I play this game with my heart and soul. So when that happens, it's second nature, and it's hard to hold back from.".

Industry observers note that cam Skattebo on doing a backflip today, days after tabling celebration: “I do whatever I can to bring the energy for the team. I play this game with my heart and soul.” pic.twitter.com/vc6qRxfk9u.

Recent findings suggest that harbaugh, meanwhile, offered a bit of a wry/forced/half smile and said, "Yeah, he couldn't help himself, could he? Just couldn't help himself.".

He couldn't help himself, could he" 😭John Harbaugh on Cam Skattebo's backflip pic.twitter.com/hN1dC75Fxo.

Recent findings suggest that for now, though, Harbaugh will at least be relieved Skattebo made up for his mistake with a major run and didn't get hurt celebrating. Only time will tell if this was a one-off or if the backflip celebration — like Skattebo on that crucial play — cannot be contained.

Ranking the NBA's most hopeless teams: Which franchise is in the bleakest situation? And who can't fix it?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2152 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Milwaukee Bucks faced Giannis Antetokounmpo as an opponent for the first time on Wednesday, and it didn't go well.
  • Recent findings suggest that the question here is how bleak.
  • To be clear here, we are operating in terms of championship equity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Milwaukee Bucks faced Giannis Antetokounmpo as an opponent for the first time on Wednesday, and it didn't go well. Though the final score highlighted only a seven-point margin, the Miami Heat led by 26 after three quarters and were never in much danger. The defeat dropped the Bucks to 1-14 on the season. The greatest player in their franchise's history now wears another jersey, and they're at the beginning of what figures to be a very long rebuild. Things are bleak.

Recent findings suggest that the question here is how bleak. Milwaukee knew it would spend this season in the cellar. It probably expects to live there for a few years. But how far away from winning seriously are the Bucks really? Are they further from genuine contention than any other team in the NBA? Who, right now, has the bleakest long-term outlook?

To be clear here, we are operating in terms of championship equity. We don't care if you have a chance to be a plucky .500 team. No, the barometer we're using here is how likely each team is to reach a conference finals in the next five seasons. We're accounting not only for players on the existing roster, but long-term financial flexibility, available draft assets and the competence of the front office helming these organizations. With all of that in mind, let's rank the NBA's most hopeless long-term outlooks.

Sources indicate that the broad sentiment following their punishment for circumventing the salary cap with Kawhi Leonard was that the Clippers faced the bleakest future in the entire NBA. That's probably overstating things slightly.

Remember, we're talking about a Los Angeles team here. Someone, inevitably, is going to want to play for them. All it takes is one player bucking the league-wide trend against superstar free agency and they're back in business. They have an owner who will spare no expense in pursuit of wins, and there's a 26-year-old All-Star in Darius Garland already on the roster. Couple that with the hope generated by No. 5 overall pick Keaton Wagler, and while the path here is extremely narrow, it exists. If the Brooklyn Nets could build a contender without draft picks in the late 2010s, it's theoretically possible for the Clippers to do the same.

Of course, the Nets weren't subject to that league-wide pivot away from free agency. They didn't have to trade picks to get Kevin Durant or Kyrie Irving in the door. It's much, much harder nowadays to import talent like that without sacrificing picks that the Clippers frankly don't have. The five first-round picks they were docked in the Leonard investigation left them fully Stepien-locked: while they will have (not especially valuable) first-round picks in odd-numbered years moving forward, they can't trade any of them yet.

Sources indicate that there's also the reputational hit the Clippers just took. Will players interested in winning want to risk their careers on a team that cheated? Can the Clippers even appeal to such players given their asset deficit? These are going to be real hurdles. Their path to the conference finals might rely on a star who's not especially competitive. After all, anyone serious about winning could find a team closer to doing so.

In a recent development, they're a blank slate with one very promising prospect. Darius Acuff is putting up star box-score numbers in his rookie season. That's by no means a guarantee of future stardom, of course. He's as inefficient as you'd expect a rookie to be on this volume. He's taking more shots per game than Jalen Brunson, Tyrese Maxey or Dwyane Wade ever did over a full season. But Acuff has a path to becoming one of the NBA's best offensive point guards. These aren't totally empty calories.

According to recent reports, there's nothing else here. No other notable prospects aside from a handful of likely long-term bench youngsters (Dylan Cardwell, Maxime Raynaud, Emanuel Sharp). Sacramento mostly controls its own picks (aside from the 2031 swap it inexplicably gave San Antonio in the DeMar DeRozan sign-and-trade), but that means less than it used to in the lottery reform era. Its books slowly clean up in the offseasons to come, with Zach LaVine and De'Andre Hunter expiring after this season and Domantas Sabonis and Malik Monk joining them in the summer of 2028, but Sacramento's forays into cap space have typically been unsuccessful. This isn't exactly a desirable destination. That's what happens when you miss the playoffs 19 times in 20 years.

Recent findings suggest that that's what separates Sacramento from fellow "one possible star, otherwise blank slate" candidates like the Chicago Bulls. With the hire of Bryson Graham to run basketball operations, the Bulls at least appear to be trending towards becoming a normal organization. Normalcy has eternally eluded Sacramento. The burden of proof is on the Kings. When you've been a mess for 20 years, it's on you to prove that you've cleaned up your act. We'll trust the Kings when they've earned it and not a second sooner.

Industry observers note that for now, they can at least start by actually keeping their success stories in the building. They've kept only one first-round pick this decade through the end of his rookie contract: Keegan Murray, who is now pretty substantially overpaid. Meanwhile, Tyrese Haliburton has blossomed into a superstar in Indiana, while their entire 2021 draft class (Davion Mitchell and Neemias Queta) now starts for Eastern Conference championship hopefuls. They had the unanimous Coach of the Year and the Executive of the Year and fired both within two years. The Kings can't help themselves.

Recent findings suggest that there's far more talent in the cupboard here than in Sacramento, but the same organizational concerns apply. The Joe Dumars regime makes mistakes -- the two-year minimum for DeAndre Jordan, not waiting until after the 2025 Finals to trade Indiana its 2026 pick back, everything Shamit Dua has reported about the infamous Derik Queen trade -- that typical teams would never dream of.

It has been revealed that there is not a discernible plan here besides, seemingly, "acquire players who can put the ball through the hoop." There are a lot of decent individual creators on this roster. None of them synergize well because so few of them can consistently make 3s and all of them are on-ball players with stylistic clashes. The Pelicans have seemingly made the determination, for instance, that Queen cannot play significant minutes alongside Zion Williamson. That's a reasonable choice... but then why is Williamson still on the team? Or, if the Pelicans view him as a fixture, why make such a risky trade for Queen in the first place?

The trickle-down effect of putting all of these dribblers on the same team is that none of them seem happy to be on it. Dejounte Murray asked for a trade. Jordan Poole is making googly eyes at the Warriors. Trey Murphy has reportedly signaled a desire to move. What is the initiative here? What kind of team are the Pelicans trying to build? What do they view as their path to genuine winning?

That's what distinguishes New Orleans from Sacramento. If the Kings get a few more high draft picks and use them on players that complement Acuff, I'd see the vision. It would require Acuff becoming an All-NBA scorer and those picks hitting, but I see the sort of teams they could build, even if they're unlikely to actually do so. I have no earthly idea what the Pelicans would do with a few high picks because talent is not right now the problem. It's how they're using and nurturing it. It's just hard to envision a team with so little understanding of how to balance skill sets and bring out the best in their players making a serious playoff push. Something significant in the organization would have to change.

They're the best team on this list in the present, and they've clawed their way back to .500 after a miserable start that included leaks about the team's lack of a point guard. Again, we're dealing in upside here. That's what the Suns lack.

Industry observers note that they control none of their own first-round picks in the seven-year tradable window except for their 2032 selection... which is frozen because they spent the 2024-25 season above the second apron. Even if they had picks, the Suns under Matt Ishbia have never displayed any discipline in using them. Ishbia traded nearly a full draft for Kevin Durant mere days after acquiring the team, spent an unprotected 2031 pick on three far lesser choices that amounted to Mark Williams and a Jusuf Nurkić cap dump, and then spent their 2033 pick as soon as they could access it to get Miles Bridges, whom they've been meaningfully better without thus far this season.

The most talented players here are all right around their physical peaks. Devin Booker is 30. Dillon Brooks turns 31 this season, and Bridges turns 29. They're going to get worse, not better, and without draft picks, their means of replacing them are minimal. Even the diamonds they've dug out of the rough are on the older side. Collin Gillespie is 27. Jordan Goodwin is 28. The truly young players, like Khaman Maluach and Rasheer Fleming, have thus far underwhelmed. The younger, star-level talent here is Jalen Green, who plays Booker's position and has been a disaster on both ends this season. Why exactly is he still starting over Gillespie? Are the Suns just trying to salvage his trade value?

Sources indicate that teams like the Clippers, Kings and Pelicans are at least young enough and financially flexible enough to grow. The Suns, at least from an asset and financial standpoint, are essentially all-in on a Play-In-caliber roster. That Play-In-caliber roster is going to get worse as it gets older and more expensive and, without access to top talent in the draft, replenishing it is going to be borderline impossible.

It has been revealed that the Bucks cherry-pick traits from all of our other selections. The Clippers circumvented the cap; the Bucks are getting investigated for doing so with Gary Trent Jr. The Pelicans have a roster full of overlapping skill sets; the Bucks have a million shooting guards, which made the decision to re-sign Trent for $64 million all the stranger. The Suns don't control any of their own picks and the Bucks won't until 2031 at the earliest. The Kings have the NBA's least-successful owner in Vivek Ranadivé, while the Bucks may have the NFL's in Jimmy Haslam, though he technically won't become governor until 2028 due to Milwaukee's bizarre ownership structure (another point against them, as successful teams tend to have stable leadership rather than rotating five-year terms).

Who is going to be the best player on the team in five years? Brayden Burries is the best long-term prospect, but he profiles as more of a high-end role player. Tyler Herro was an All-Star in the sense that Norman Powell and D'Angelo Russell were All-Stars: they put up big numbers in a weak Eastern Conference. Kel'El Ware was the lottery ticket from the Giannis Antetokounmpo trade and he's been so bad that he's somehow playing less than he did on a Heat team that was trying to win. Without access to their own picks or a market that tends to draw free agents, they're basically hoping someone internal (Nate Ament? Ryan Rollins?) breaks out or that they hit on a pick far later than you should rely on.

According to recent reports, you could argue that just by virtue of being in the Eastern Conference, the Bucks have a cleaner path to the final four than those West teams do because they don't have to worry about Victor Wembanyama or the specter of healthier versions of the Oklahoma City Thunder down the line. Vikings utilize NFL's obscure fair-catch kick rule to attempt 71-yard field goal against 49ers

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The game between the Vikings and the 49ers got a little confusing toward the end of the first half on Sunday night when Minnesota decided to take advantage of an obscure NFL rule known as the fair-catch kick.
  • With 11 seconds left to play in the first half, the 49ers were facing a fourth-and-19 from their own 11-yard line, which was an obvious punting situation for San Francisco.
  • Sources indicate that basically, the rule goes like this: If a team fair catches a punt, they're allowed to attempt a free kick on the next play.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The game between the Vikings and the 49ers got a little confusing toward the end of the first half on Sunday night when Minnesota decided to take advantage of an obscure NFL rule known as the fair-catch kick.

With 11 seconds left to play in the first half, the 49ers were facing a fourth-and-19 from their own 11-yard line, which was an obvious punting situation for San Francisco. Vikings returner Myles Price called for a fair catch on the play, and that's where the rarely used fair-catch kick came in.

Sources indicate that basically, the rule goes like this: If a team fair catches a punt, they're allowed to attempt a free kick on the next play. The kick isn't a typical field goal, either. The defense has to line up 10 yards off the ball — similar to a kickoff — and the defense is NOT allowed to try to block the kick. The "free kick" is more like a kickoff, except the kicker has to attempt the field goal off the ground, and there's also a holder (the kicker also has the option to dropkick the ball, but that almost never happens).

Here's how the NFL describes the rule:.

Industry observers note that "After a fair catch, the receiving team has the option to put the ball in play by a snap or a fair-catch kick (field goal attempt), with fair-catch kick lines established ten yards apart. All general rules apply as for a field goal attempt from scrimmage. The clock starts when the ball is kicked. (No tee permitted.)".

In a recent development, now that you know how the rule works, let's get back to the game. Price actually called for a fair catch from his own 40-yard line, which meant that if the Vikings wanted to take advantage of the rule, they would have to attempt a 71-YARD FIELD GOAL. With the game being played in Mexico City, which sits at an elevation of 7,350 feet, that adds about five yards to a kicker's natural distance, so the Vikings decided to send out Will Reichard for the potentially record-setting kick.

According to the broadcast, Reichard hit from 68 yards in warm-ups, so the Vikings thought he could hit from 71, and it ALMOST HAPPENED. Reichard's kick only fell about a yard short.

Industry observers note that will Reichard comes up just short on a 71-yard fair catch free kick in Mexico City. Mike Tirico with the SNF call for NBC. 🏈🎙️ pic.twitter.com/q3BDFyVWBP.

According to recent reports, if the kick had gone in, it would have counted in the record book as the longest field goal in NFL history. But since he missed, Cam Little still holds the record at 68 yards.

There have only been 10 field goal attempts ever from 70 yards or longer, and Little actually had one of them back in Week 3 when he just barely missed a kick against the Patriots. Out of the other nine attempts, four of them came on a fair-catch kick, including Reichards'.

In a recent development, the fair-catch kick is rare: There have only been 21 attempts ever in the Super Bowl era, and only one kicker has actually made one over the past 40 years (Cameron Dicker in December 2024). Reichard had a chance at NFL history on Sunday night, but he came up about a yard short. Reichard also missed a 55-yard attempt in the first half.

The Brooklyn Nets are no strangers to losing games this season, as they fell to 3-11 on Wednesday night, but in a season filled with lopsided defeats, losing by 30 points to the Chicago Bulls stood out as a new low point.

In a recent development, the Bulls also entered Wednesday's game at 3-10 on the season, operating as one of the league's worst teams so far, but Chicago exploded for 137 points against the Nets, with eight players reaching double figures. While Chicago's biggest glitch has come on the defensive end this season, the Bulls haven't exactly been lighting opponents up offensively, sitting 23rd in the league in offensive rating.

The Nets' complete inability to put up a resistance against the Bulls rang alarm bells in Brooklyn and had veteran Julius Randle calling out his team for an "embarrassing" and "unacceptable" performance.

"I've been in the league for 13 years... that's one of the worst games I've ever been a part of."Julius Randle didn't hold back after the Nets’ 30-point loss to Bulls. 😳 pic.twitter.com/s3YQ8TxP35.

"The main struggle? I don't know, that was embarrassing," Randle noted after the game. "Been in the league for 13 years and that's one of the worst games I've ever been a part of. And not because of the score. You lose by 30 sometimes -- it's just a bad night -- but it's how we did it. That just, it wasn't cool. Nothing about it was cool. We gotta find a way to figure out the root of it or whatever, but that just is unacceptable.".

Considering Randle has been on his fair share of bad basketball teams over his career in Los Angeles, Newly introduced Orleans and New York, that's saying something.

There are five teams that have separated themselves from the pack at the bottom of the NBA in terms of defense and the Nets are one of them with a 119.0 defensive rating (26th in the league). No one expected much of Brooklyn on that end of the floor with the roster they've assembled, but it's one thing to have lesser talent on the defensive end; it's another to combine that with a general lack of effort.

This early in the season, the latter is a much larger concern and the Nets have now given up at least 124 points in five of their last six games. If they were able to shrug off some of those lopsided losses to quality teams as life in the NBA, Wednesday was proof that their problems extend far beyond just some schedule losses.

Giving up 137 to a Bulls team that's been similarly bad this year is, in Randle's words, unacceptable. The concern is that no one in Brooklyn, including Randle, seems quite sure what the exact problem is or how to fix it.

#164856. Why a long-term mega deal for Tarik Skubal isn't actually all that risky

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1273 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

Why a long-term mega deal for Tarik Skubal isn't actually all that risky

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1273 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The big prize of this free agent class, ace lefty and two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, has landed with the Mets on a nine-year, $450 million deal.
  • The knee-jerk reaction to a contract of this size in many corners will be that he won't possibly be "worth" that much and that such a deal would be a huge "risk" to the signing team.
  • There's risk for the team on every contract, especially pitchers, of course, but in Skubal, the Mets are getting a surefire ace for nearly a decade.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The big prize of this free agent class, ace lefty and two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, has landed with the Mets on a nine-year, $450 million deal.

The knee-jerk reaction to a contract of this size in many corners will be that he won't possibly be "worth" that much and that such a deal would be a huge "risk" to the signing team.

Let's stop right there. I don't think it's all that risky. There's risk for the team on every contract, especially pitchers, of course, but in Skubal, the Mets are getting a surefire ace for nearly a decade.

Let's examine some of the reasons why such an enormous deal isn't actually that dangerous.

Industry observers note that since returning from surgery in 2023, Skubal has been absurdly good. Across his ages 26-29 seasons, he's made 103 starts and has gone 50-20 with a 2.47 ERA (169 ERA+), 0.92 WHIP and 757 strikeouts in 626 ⅓ innings. He's only walked 109, or 1.6 per nine innings. He rarely gets hit hard, he rarely gives up many runs, he strikes out a high number of hitters and rarely walks any. Simply, he's been good at everything.

The recent track record here notes this is the best pitcher in baseball, at least in the long view (we could argue Paul Skenes was better in 2025 and Jacob Misiorowski was better in 2026, to name two examples, but if we looked at 2023-present, it isn't all that close).

There isn't a dropoff in the postseason, either. In eight playoff starts, Skubal has a 2.13 ERA, 0.79 WHIP and 70 strikeouts against nine unintentional walks in 50 ⅔ innings.

In a recent development, he's stellar. Pretty much all the time.

According to recent reports, also, the career workload isn't anything to be concerned about. Skubal heads to his age-30 season now with only 925 ⅓ innings in the regular season. Even counting the playoffs doesn't get Skubal to 1,000 innings at the major-league level. Let's go back to Skenes. He's only 24 years old and already has 495 career innings. Another ace? Justin Verlander had 1,553 ⅔ career innings through his age-29 season.

There just isn't a ton of tread on these Skubal tires.

We'll hear plenty of consternation about Skubal being 30 years old next season as it relates to signing a long-term deal. We'll also hear people say a deal is risky due to his injury history. He had Tommy John surgery in college, flexor tendon surgery in 2022 and arthroscopic surgery (a fresh procedure using a Nanoscope) in 2026.

The simple matter is that pretty much every pitcher nowadays has had some sort of surgery on his arm, notably the elbow, and we've seen pitchers time and again bounce back after elbow surgery to perform at a high level.

Industry observers note that skubal just did it. He only missed roughly six weeks after his procedure this past season. He came back to make 19 starts after the surgery and posted a 2.73 ERA with 141 strikeouts in 115 ⅓ innings.

According to recent reports, I mentioned Verlander above. Skubal is a multi-time Cy Young winner, so it's acceptable to look at some of the best pitchers in baseball and how they aged into their late-30s in recent memory.

Again, Skubal will be in his age-30 season in 2027. His nine-year deal means it'll run through his age-38 season.

Recent findings suggest that for those so worried about the long-term finances of the Cohen family, are you sure you're really worried that Skubal won't be productive through five, six or even all nine years of that deal? Given his track record, talent, pitching arsenal, relatively low workload given his age and how well some of the best pitchers have fared through their mid-30s, he actually seems like a great bet.

Sources indicate that A decade ago, the common talking point was that long and huge deals for pitchers never age well. That isn't actually the case, for the most part. Here are some of the biggest pitcher contracts of all time and how they unfolded (or are unfolding).

It has been revealed that yoshinobu Yamamoto, Dodgers, 12 years, $325 million -- He came over from Japan for his age-25 season, so this one was a different animal. Still, it sure doesn't seem like it'll be a bad deal, does it?

Sources indicate that gerrit Cole, Yankees, 9 years, $324 million -- Through six years of the deal, Cole has missed a chunk of time due to Tommy John surgery. He's also won a Cy Young, finished top four in Cy Young voting three times, been worth 22.4 WAR and was the ace of an American League pennant winner.

Stephen Strasburg, Nationals, 7 years, $245 million -- Here's the bust. Strasburg was never healthy again after the 2019 World Series title run. Still, the Nationals wouldn't have that title without him.

In a recent development, justin Verlander, Tigers, 10 years, $219.5 million -- This was the deal that ran from 2010-19. During this deal, Verlander won two Cy Youngs (one in the second year of the deal, one in the final year), a World Series, three pennants, 160 games and led the league in pitcher WAR three times.

Max Fried, Yankees, 8 years, $218 million -- It's only been two years, but Fried is 24-10 with a 2.83 ERA and finished fourth in AL Cy Young voting in his first year.

Recent findings suggest that david Price, Red Sox, 7 years, $217 million -- He won a World Series in the third year of the contract. Overall, he was 53-26 with a 3.78 ERA (118 ERA+) through the course of the deal.

Corbin Burnes, Diamondbacks, 6 years, $210 million -- Burnes had his first year of the deal interrupted by Tommy John surgery. He had a 2.66 ERA through 11 starts prior to the injury. The jury's still out, but he heads to his age-32 season fully recovered now.

Zack Greinke, 6 years, $206.5 million -- Over the course of this deal, Greinke was 77-39 with a 3.55 ERA (125 ERA+) and 19.9 WAR. He had a fourth-place Cy Young finish in there.

Recent findings suggest that CC Sabathia, 9 years, $202 million -- The Yankees won the World Series in Sabathia's first year there and he started the deal with three straight top-four Cy Young finishes. Overall, during this deal, he was 120-73 with 27.1 WAR and had five straight 200-plus inning seasons.

Max Scherzer, 7 years, $191.4 million -- During this contract, Scherzer won two Cy Youngs, a World Series title and 99 games with a 2.75 ERA. He posted 41.8 WAR. In the seven years on this deal, Scherzer finished in the top five in Cy Young voting six times, with 2020 being the outlier.

It has been revealed that we can close with this. Some people might not care for such a measure, particularly the salary cap crowd who will be worried about the owners paying too much. Regardless, let's stick with the general belief that each individual WAR (1.0 WAR) is worth a bit over $8 million per season.

Industry observers note that by this measure, Skubal was worth $48.4 million in 2024, $53.7 million in 2025 and $41.7 million last season. Putting aside how much less money he actually made than what he was doing on the field, and knowing everything laid out above, I'll ask a simple question:.

Are you sure a 9-year, $450 million deal for this guy is a "risk?".

I think we could argue that it'll be a bargain.

#164854. Tech Report: Steelers gave DK Metcalf $150 million, traded George Pickens. Now they're paying for both decisions

Tech Report: Steelers gave DK Metcalf $150 million, traded George Pickens. Now they're paying for both decisions

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1249 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There was a time the Steelers were really, really good at drafting and developing wide receivers.
  • In fact, since drafting Pickens with the 52nd overall pick in 2022, Pittsburgh has selected exactly three receivers: Roman Wilson (third round, '24), Germie Bernard (second round, '26) and Kaden Wetjen (fourth round, '26).
  • Sources indicate that consider what the Steelers have done the last two offseasons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There was a time the Steelers were really, really good at drafting and developing wide receivers. Hines Ward, Plaxico Burress, Santonio Holmes, Mike Wallace, Emmanuel Sanders, Antonio Brown, JuJu Smith-Schuster, Diontae Johnson, George Pickens. Of those nine names, two were first-round picks, six were Day 2 picks, and Brown was a sixth-rounder.

In fact, since drafting Pickens with the 52nd overall pick in 2022, Pittsburgh has selected exactly three receivers: Roman Wilson (third round, '24), Germie Bernard (second round, '26) and Kaden Wetjen (fourth round, '26). The philosophy, it seems, is less about developing receivers than trading for established players and paying a premium to do so. (By the way, as we've written previously, these struggles have not been limited to just pass catchers.).

Sources indicate that consider what the Steelers have done the last two offseasons. In March 2025, they traded a second-round pick as part of a package to acquire DK Metcalf, then gave him a five-year, $150 million contract. A year later, they traded for Michael Pittman Jr. and signed him to a three-year, $59 million deal.

It has been revealed that that's $209 million in total contract commitments to two receivers, and through 11 weeks of the 2026 season, they have combined for 523 yards and two touchdowns. Pittman has played just three games because of injuries, while Metcalf has as many touchdown receptions this season as games he's been suspended since arriving in Pittsburgh. (Two. The answer for both is two.) And that doesn't include Sunday's ejection in Philadelphia, which could mean we'll have to patch the "Days since DK was suspended" sign once again when the league is done with him.

It's also not a stretch to suggest that the Steelers are worse off at receiver than they were before all this started.

In a recent development, early in his career, Metcalf was one of the NFL's most dangerous targets. In 2020, his second season in Seattle, he caught 83 passes for 1,303 yards and 10 touchdowns. He was always a straight-line player – but he consistently won with his physicality, size and 4.3 speed.

That was six years ago. He had two more 1,000-plus-yard seasons in Seattle, but 2020 turned out to be his most productive year in the league. He's been an unrecognizable shell of that player in this season.

So far this season, Metcalf is averaging 43.4 yards per game, and his 1.16 yards per route is easily the lowest of his career. For perspective, he averaged more than two yards per route in both 2020 and 2023.

Recent findings suggest that put another way: The Steelers paid $30 million annually for a receiver who has combined for 1,280 yards in 25 games. Here's where it gets worse: Among 16 veteran receivers we looked at who were acquired via trade or free agency between 2022 and 2025, Metcalf gave his team the least production for its money in his first season. Stefon Diggs, Jerry Jeudy and Darnell Mooney all provided considerably more bang for the buck, despite signing smaller contracts.

Let's dig a little further. For every $1 million in annual salary, Metcalf averaged just 1.89 receiving yards per game in 2025. Jeudy, who made $17.5 million annually, averaged 72.3 yards per game, or 4.13 yards for every $1 million. Mooney was even better: 62 yards per game on a $13 million annual deal, more than twice the production per dollar Pittsburgh got from Metcalf.

And it's gotten worse in 2026. Metcalf is now averaging just 1.45 receiving yards per game for every $1 million. In other words, the Steelers are paying the same price for 23% less production than they got a year ago.

According to recent reports, if the Metcalf trade was supposed to solve Pittsburgh's WR1 problem, acquiring Pittman was supposed to address everything else. The Steelers needed someone who could consistently get open, move the chains and take some pressure off Metcalf.

It has been revealed that pittman had been a dependable receiver in Indianapolis, including a 109-catch, 1,152-yard season in 2023. But his production declined over the next two years, and injuries have limited him to seven catches for 89 yards since arriving in Pittsburgh.

In a recent development, injuries happen, sure. And the Steelers gave up next to nothing to acquire him, essentially moving down 16 spots in the 2026 draft, from No. 214 to No. 230. The financial commitment, however, is another matter. The organization now has two expensive veteran receivers and little in the way of production to show for it.

Recent findings suggest that so while Pittsburgh was overpaying for Metcalf in 2025, Washington acquired Deebo Samuel from San Francisco for a fifth-round pick. Samuel caught 72 passes for 727 yards and five touchdowns last season and added value as a runner.

Sources indicate that latest England took a different approach, signing Stefon Diggs to a three-year, $63.5 million contract. Diggs responded with 85 receptions for 1,013 yards, despite coming off a season-ending knee injury in 2024.

Neither receiver required anything close to the combination of draft capital and long-term financial commitment Metcalf received.

Hindsight, you might say, is 20/20, and anybody can cherry-pick examples that worked out after the fact. Fair enough. But we don't know many folks who thought at the time that Metcalf was worth $30 million a year. Or that Michael Pittman, who is a possession receiver at best when he's healthy, had earned a fresh deal.

Recent findings suggest that and we'll grant you this: None of this means Diggs or Samuel would've produced the same numbers in Pittsburgh, which now seems like where passing offenses go to die. But it's difficult to ignore the financial flexibility those teams maintained while getting meaningful contributions from those veteran additions.

And then there's Pickens, which might be the most hilariously frustrating part of this saga for Steelers fans.

The team had understandably grown tired of Pickens' mood swings, which often manifested themselves as inconsistent effort and dumb penalties. So two months after acquiring Metcalf, the Steelers traded Pickens to Dallas rather than deal with the nonsense for another season.

According to recent reports, pickens responded with 93 catches for 1,429 yards and nine touchdowns in 2025. He already has 780 yards and six touchdowns through 10 games in 2026. Metcalf, meanwhile, is one of the NFL's most ineffective receivers, and the cherry on top is that he's been a bigger headache in Pittsburgh than Pickens ever was. Last December, the NFL suspended him for two games after a physical confrontation with a fan in Detroit. And then, on Sunday, Metcalf was ejected after getting into it with Eagles defensive back Cooper DeJean.

So let's recap: Pittsburgh moved on from Pickens because he was a pain in the ass, then paid Metcalf $150 million to be invisible as a playmaker and front-and-center as a distraction. Make it make sense.

It has been revealed that now the Steelers have committed another $59 million to Pittman, who has spent most Sundays this fall on the sidelines in sweats. Aaron Rodgers is done after the season, which means that whoever is under center in 2027 could inherit one of the worst offenses in the league.

For all the money and draft picks the Steelers have wasted trying to fix their receiver room, perhaps the most damning indictment is this: A franchise that once set the standard for finding and developing young receivers now seems incapable of doing either.

Sources indicate that the trophies won by Franco Baresi, who has died at the age of 66, are their own monument to the AC Milan and Italy defender’s greatness. Six times a Serie A champion, five as captain, three European Cup-winning campaigns, 10 other winners’ medals and the distinction of being a member of Italy squads that finished in first, second and third places at World Cup tournaments demonstrate that his career, in a significantly more meritocratic era, stand alongside the giants even if the bias towards attacking virtuosos denied him the Ballon d’Or his talent deserved.

Yet they do not tell us why the grief, so tangible in Milan and beyond today, transcends tribal rivalry. It would be unfair to say that he transformed the art of Italian defending. Gaetano Scirea, the elegant Juventus sweeper who kept the 21-year-old Baresi confined to the bench when Italy won their third World Cup in 1982, had a surplus of natural ability, composure and intelligence. He did not need the raw-elbowed brutality of Claudio Gentile, heir to generations of Italian defenders influenced by the post-war influx of players brought up in the traditions of Argentina and Uruguay.

Both clubs now have upcoming managers, with Xabi Alonso taking over at Chelsea and former Manchester United boss Ruben Amorim now at the helm at AC Milan. These sides met in pre-season last year, with Chelsea winning 4-1 at Stamford Bridge. At that time, now-Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca was in charge whilst Max Allegri, who is now at Napoli, was leading AC Milan. The last time they met competitively was during the 2022/23 Champions League season, with Chelsea winning both games.

Chelsea lost 1-0 to AC Milan’s Serie A rivals Juventus on Wednesday in Hong Kong, in which Danny Welbeck made his first Chelsea appearance after joining from Brighton in the last week.

In a recent development, “We want to have a great team spirit and that is built on a daily basis with a great culture in the building,” Alonso noted in his pre-match press conference. “That helps in the moment you have to compete. You feel better having that togetherness, trust, and the bonds between the players are so vital to ultimately building a winning mentality, and a team that can compete anywhere. So the football side is so important, but the mental side is as important. And the strength of the team is the most important. We have been able to train and prepare [during pre-season] and I am very happy with the attitude and personality, we know that it is a very important part of this tour.”.

In a recent development, it has been another busy week on the transfer front for Chelsea; not only has Welbeck arrived over the last week but so too have Jordan Henderson and Valentin Barco. Alonso’s men have two more games after this against Johor Darul Ta’zim and Real Sociedad before getting their Premier League campaign under way with a derby against Fulham at Craven Cottage.

Sources indicate that AC Milan finished fifth in Serie A last season to earn a spot in the Europa League last season. Their significant-money acquisition this summer as been Portuguese striker Goncalo Ramos from PSG. They have played two pre-season friendlies so far, which have both ended in draws; 2-2 against Celtic and then 1-1 against city rivals Inter. They kick off their Serie A campaign at Torino on August 23.

Breaking: NBA's eight biggest disappointments through one month: Injury bug, same old East and an underwhelming champ

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we're roughly one month into the 2026-27 NBA season, and things are going pretty well in certain respects.
  • In other areas, things are going … not so well.
  • It has been revealed that there have been so many players impacted by various injuries that it's almost hard to keep track.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we're roughly one month into the 2026-27 NBA season, and things are going pretty well in certain respects. Luka Dončić and the Lakers are off to a hot start in Los Angeles. Victor Wembanyama and the Spurs have picked up right where they left off after last season's Finals trip. And the Celtics are battling the upcoming-look Sixers at the top of the Eastern Conference.

In other areas, things are going … not so well. Below are the eight biggest disappointments so far this season.

It has been revealed that there have been so many players impacted by various injuries that it's almost hard to keep track. Jalen Duren (hamstring) has missed almost the entire season in Detroit. Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody are still recovering from knee injuries and have yet to play for Golden State, while Steph Curry is now out with an abdominal tear and Kristaps Porziņģis stepped away from basketball. After sitting out all of last season with an Achilles tear, Tyrese Haliburton is at the moment dealing with a hamstring problem. Brandon Ingram (Achilles) hasn't made his debut for the Clippers. Austin Reaves is out with a heel injury. Anthony Edwards underwent knee surgery and will miss a chunk of time for the Wolves, and it seems unlikely that Donte DiVincenzo (Achilles) will play this season, even though he remains hopeful that he will. Paolo Banchero remains sidelined with an ankle sprain. Ja Morant is out with a hamstring strain. Ben Simmons didn't play a single game for the Kings before tearing his Achilles. Kawhi Leonard (knee) is once again on the shelf in Toronto. And the reeling Jazz are without Jaren Jackson Jr (knee), Lauri Markkanen (hand) and Jusuf Nurkic (toe).

It's all a huge bummer for the players, their teams and fans of hoops in general. But no team has been hurt more on the injury front than the Thunder.

The disappointment here is how unkind fate has been to OKC. The Thunder were close to fully healthy when the season started — and then far from it not long after it began. When OKC beat the Spurs in San Antonio in the season opener — after losing four of five regular season games to them last season, as well as falling to the Spurs in the Western Conference Finals — it felt like a statement that the Thunder were back and we were in for an epic battle between the two teams over who would rule the West.

And then all of that was stripped away. Just three games into the season, Jalen Williams — who missed much of last season due to injury — suffered a gruesome fall and had to undergo surgery for a fractured fibula as well as reconstruction of ankle ligaments. In that same fateful game, Cason Wallace tore his labrum and later had shoulder surgery. They haven't been officially ruled out, but if either of them plays basketball again this season, it will be a surprise. Making matters worse, Chet Holmgren tore a tendon in his knee and "underwent a biological treatment" to address it. He'll miss approximately two months, but the Thunder do expect him to return. That's what passes for good news in OKC these days.

The Thunder are — or were — the deepest team in the NBA. That's a credit to what Sam Presti built. But even OKC has its limits. Losing three of five starters is tough to overcome, even when you're led by the reigning back-to-back MVP in Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. That doesn't mean the Thunder (currently 9-6 and eighth in the West) can't still make a deep playoff run, but the odds of them doing so — and of them fighting the Spurs all season for the top spot — got a lot longer.

We were told that this was finally the season that the East returned to its former glory. We were told that the conference would be loaded. We were wrong. (Full disclosure while putting a palm to my face: I might have done some of that telling.).

Through the first month, the East has been mostly underwhelming. Eight of the 15 teams are below .500. The conference has a combined 17-37 record against the West. Only one of the top seven teams in net rating — the Celtics — plays in the East. Five of the top six teams by point differential play in the West.

The defending champion Knicks are 8-6. The Cavaliers, who made it to last season's Eastern Conference Finals and had championship aspirations of their own, are 8-8. The Magic, Raptors and Pacers — who right now occupy the eight, nine and 10 seeds — all have losing records. By contrast, the worst play-in team in the West right now is Golden State at 8-7. That record would be good enough for the seven seed if they played in the East.

According to recent reports, but maybe we shouldn't be surprised. Since the 1999-2000 season, the West has had the better overall record in all but three campaigns. Maybe next year the East will finally snap out of its funk, but don't bet on it.

Recent findings suggest that the Jazz just picked up back-to-back road wins in L.A. over the Lakers and Clippers, but that doesn't begin to dig them out of the deep hole they've made for themselves. The Jazz were gearing up to be competitive in the West this season. So much for that. Like the Thunder, injuries have not been kind to them. Nurkic has yet to play a single game this season, while Markkanen and JJJ have missed significant time with maladies of their own. What looked like a formidable frontcourt has been decimated.

Still, it's hard to believe how bad the Jazz have been in pretty much every facet. Their first win came in the second game of the season, a one-point squeaker over the Pelicans. It took until mid-November to end an ugly 12-game losing streak and pick up their second and third wins. They're 25th in net rating and point differential. The season has barely begun, and it's already basically wait until next year for the Jazz.

Recent findings suggest that the NBA panicked and tried to solve for a problem that wasn't actually an problem, except for a small fragment of people who care more about optics than the product itself. And so the league enacted lottery reform and the new 3-2-1 system was put in place. This was ostensibly designed to prevent tanking, incentivize winning and bring greater parity to the league. Oops.

The Hornets, Wizards, Bulls, Nets and Bucks are all well underwater in the East. The Pelicans and Clippers are drowning in the West, while the Kings and Jazz are even worse. What the league failed to account for is that some of these teams are just organically bad — and now they will have decreased odds at getting better.

Under the old system, the Grizzlies would be pretty thrilled to see the Jazz struggling since Memphis has Utah's first-round pick in the upcoming draft as part of the JJJ trade. Alas, after making that move, the league changed the rules, which means the Grizzlies can pick no higher than sixth now as a consequence of the fresh system preventing a team from picking in the top five in three consecutive drafts. Since the Jazz picked in the top five in each of the last two drafts, that means the Grizzlies are now out of luck with that Utah pick this time around. Womp, womp for them.

Sources indicate that and on top of it all, fans of bad teams were robbed of the entertaining-in-its-own-way race to the bottom to maximize lottery odds, giving supporters a small silver lining in the otherwise gray clouds of their season. RIP Tank Watch.

Recent findings suggest that when aren't the Kings disappointing? Aside from their unsightly 1-13 record, the Sacramento front office continues to make baffling decisions. The Kings originally acquired Nique Clifford from the Thunder for a Spurs 2027 first-round pick. Sacramento held onto Clifford for 83 games — choosing to bury him on the bench this season and play him barely six minutes per game — before shipping him back to the Thunder for two second-round picks.

So the Thunder ended up with the player and a first and the Kings ended up with two seconds.

One of these organizations is savvy and opportunistic, and the other is the Kings. It's a miracle they nailed the Darius Acuff pick.

Oof. It has not been a good season to date for Bridges. After going cold to begin their first-round playoff series against the Hawks, Bridges found his form and played well, helping the Knicks go on an epic run that ended with Newly introduced York's first championship in 53 years.

Recent findings suggest that if that hope was that Bridges would snap out of his early-season funk in similar fashion, the Knicks seem somewhat less patient these days. While head coach Mike Brown has insisted that Bridges is a starter, he has sometimes hedged his bets in crucial situations, going with Landry Shamet or Deuce McBride over Bridges when things get tight and the Knicks need more reliable offense on the floor.

Through 14 games, Bridges is averaging 7.5 points, 3.6 rebounds and 2.1 assists on 40.2/28.9/75 shooting splits. It's the lowest scoring output and the worst shooting numbers of his career. As a result, his minutes have dipped to 25.6 per contest. That's also a career low. Bridges is still a plus defender. And he's only 30. The Knicks obviously hope he'll figure it out, as he has in the past. If not, his new four-year, $150 million extension that kicked in this season will start to look worrisome.

Why are we still subjected to … [motions at everything below in the most pejorative fashion possible] ... this?

ALL 30 TEAM COURTS FOR @EMIRATES NBA CUP 2026 pic.twitter.com/RgBqe1VJCB.

Why can't whoever came up with the gorgeous GTA VI crossover court in Miami be in charge of the Cup floors instead?

The Miami Heat are rolling out the “Vice City” hardwood 😮‍💨👏(via @MiamiHEAT) pic.twitter.com/AFcyK2akaV.

Recent findings suggest that respecting the Cup would be so much easier if they'd give us more of this. Maybe they could dream up some sweet upcoming jerseys while they're at it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 2026-27 NBA season is barely a month old and trade season won't officially begin until December 15 when players signed this summer are eligible to be moved, but that doesn't stop the rumor machine from churning in the Association.
  • Sources indicate that the first 15 games of the season have been enough for some teams to learn the harsh truth about not being a contender this year, while others are off to surprisingly good starts that could turn them into midseason buyers.
  • According to recent reports, the one unknown this season is how the league's lottery reform will affect the in-season trade market.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 2026-27 NBA season is barely a month old and trade season won't officially begin until December 15 when players signed this summer are eligible to be moved, but that doesn't stop the rumor machine from churning in the Association.

Sources indicate that the first 15 games of the season have been enough for some teams to learn the harsh truth about not being a contender this year, while others are off to surprisingly good starts that could turn them into midseason buyers. That's how the trade market starts to take shape, and with a trade request already made in Fresh Orleans by Dejounte Murray and a handful of expiring contracts known to be open to moving, we can start piecing together an early look at what trade season may look like.

According to recent reports, the one unknown this season is how the league's lottery reform will affect the in-season trade market. Fewer teams will have incentive to completely bottom out, but even with teams not trying to sell everything off, there will still be enough teams trying to buy to create a market.

On Thursday, we got a fresh batch of rumors, starting with some updates on potential suitors for Murray after being sent home by the Pelicans.

In a recent development, murray makes $32.8 million this year and has a player option for $30.8 million next year that he will almost assuredly pick up. That means he's not exactly a coveted asset, and even for teams with a potential need at point guard, so far no one seems to be jumping at the opportunity to trade for the disgruntled Pelicans guard.

Two teams that were rapidly connected as potential destinations for Murray were the Suns and the Heat, both with glaring point guard needs and a desire to contend this season. However, neither team is desperate to make a move right now, according to Jake Fischer in the latest Stein Line newsletter.

Murray and Klutch Sports see Phoenix as a good landing spot, but the Suns view center as a bigger need than point guard and would demand that the Pelicans send back draft capital to take on Murray's salary, Fischer reports. Miami, meanwhile, has shown little appetite for Murray and he is not expected to be one of its trade targets because of his player option for next season that would severely limit their ability to retool the roster around Giannis Antetokounmpo.

With the two most obvious potential suitors for Murray not exactly showing a lot of excitement for bringing him in, it seems likely that Murray's trade request and absence from the Pelicans will extend for quite some time and could last all the way to the trade deadline.

The Washington Wizards are 5-11 to start the season, which makes it increasingly unlikely they will be trying to work out a long-term extension for Davis. The early returns on Washington's commitment to Trae Young have not been good, and if the Wizards are looking to acquire some assets this season, Davis makes the most sense as an expiring contract.

On the latest episode of the Hoop Collective, ESPN's Brian Windhorst offered an enhancement on Davis' market and desires for his next contract.

According to recent reports, "I think people have demand for Anthony Davis," Windhorst said. "They just don't want to give him a max extension, and I don't think he's looking for a max extension, but I do think he's looking for a lot of money.".

Industry observers note that that's not exactly groundbreaking information and any team exploring a trade for Davis will want to know what, exactly, he's looking for in his next contract. Below the max is a start, but teams are growing wary of giving out massive money to aging stars in the second apron era. Davis brings an additional level of risk to any long-term contract discussions with his injury history.

Industry observers note that that stated, he has been quite good this season -- averaging 24.6 points and 10.1 rebounds per game on solid efficiency -- and the Wizards should be shopping him to teams desperate for a center upgrade. If Phoenix is less interested in a point guard but has an appetite for a star center, perhaps the Suns could be a trade partner to offload Jalen Green's contract -- to be clear, that's not a rumor, just connecting dots between a few recent rumors.

Everything with Davis' market will come down to what Davis and Rich Paul tell teams about what they want his next contract to look like.

With Murray on the block and the Pelicans at 5-11, it's fair to wonder (again) if some of Upcoming Orleans' more intriguing players could find their way onto the trade market.

The player most teams around the league covet in Fresh Orleans is Trey Murphy III. Even though he's in the midst of a slow start to the season and at the moment dealing with knee tendonitis, other teams still covet his potential as a star on the wing given his abilities as a scorer and defender. The Pelicans also believe strongly in Murphy's upside, and unfortunately for other teams, Fischer reports Murphy -- unlike Murray -- has no desire to make a trade request.

Recent findings suggest that as such, he's going to be quite expensive to pry from the Pelicans, who "remain reluctant" to discuss trades for Murphy. Given he's their best potential trade chip, that's probably a wise approach, and New Orleans will hope some hopeful contender is desperate enough to give up a haul of assets before they consider moving him.

CBS Sports rules analyst Gene Steratore said later in the broadcast that he spoke to the NFL offices and they felt that there was not enough clear and obvious evidence to overturn the ruling on the field.

  • According to recent reports, "I did not think he lost possession of the football ...

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Seemingly everyone has an opinion about Jaguars wide receiver Parker Washington's controversial non-catch heard 'round the world from Jacksonville's 23-18 Week 11 loss to the Giants, but New York safety Jevón Holland's certainly isn't the best look.

First, here's the play in question.

According to recent reports, "I did not think he lost possession of the football ... I think it's a touchdown fellas."@GeneSteratore disagrees with the call of INCOMPLETE after review pic.twitter.com/b2T3eoe5my.

According to recent reports, the Jaguars settled for a field goal to make it 20-9, then scored a touchdown to cut the deficit to 23-18 (after a failed two-point conversion). Obviously, the non-catch loomed large, and Holland — perhaps tongue-in-cheek — suggested that if the game hadn't been close, the NFL might have flipped the call.

"The game's over -- that might have been a catch," Holland mentioned post-game, per The Athletic's Dan Duggan. "That was a hell of a play. I thought he got his foot down. I was like, 'Damn.' But then they called it out, and I was like, 'Shit, all right.' Shout-out Vegas. I don't know.".

Holland's comment likely will not go over well at league offices, which certainly want to avoid any link between sports betting influencing games or calls. To be clear, Holland was relieved when the call went Newly introduced York's way.

It has been revealed that NFL vice president of instant replay Mark Butterworth mentioned officials made the correct calls both initially and in upholding the call after Liam Coen's challenge. Even though Washington got two feet in bounds, Butterworth said, the ball was moving when he made contact with the ground.

"He needs to maintain control of the ball throughout the process of the catch," Butterworth said via the pool report.

Parker noted he "felt good about it" being a catch but emphasized that regardless of the call, the team needed to (and still needs to) move on. Teammates didn't exactly feel the same way, with safety Antonio Johnson saying the team was "devastated" to hear the call wouldn't be overturned, per ESPN.

NFL on CBS rules analyst Gene Steratore, play-by-play announcer Jim Nantz, and lead analyst J.J. Watt all believed it should have been a touchdown, while most Giants — Holland not included — believed the officials got it right.

It has been revealed that "He was out. Clear as day," noted cornerback Dru Phillips, who was covering Washington on the play, per ESPN. "And he bobbled the ball, too. So, it wouldn't have been a catch regardless.".

Even if the NFL didn't agree with Phillips on the first part, the second part was the deciding factor.

"The ball moved," John Harbaugh said in his post-game press conference. "The same exact one as Malik [Nabers] had [earlier in the game].".

Winners and losers of the Tarik Skubal signing: Blue Jays, Dodgers strike out; David Stearns looks nervous

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (777 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the best player in a thin free agent class came off the board Sunday evening.
  • Industry observers note that the $450 million contract shatters the previous record for a pitcher, which is Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million contract with the Dodgers, Skubal's most recent team.
  • Here now are our winners and losers from Skubal's monster contract with the Mets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the best player in a thin free agent class came off the board Sunday evening. Two-time Cy Young winning left-hander Tarik Skubal has agreed to a record nine-year, $450 million contract with the New York Mets. There's a $45 million signing bonus and $30 million in deferred payments. The team has not yet confirmed the signing but that should happen soon.

Industry observers note that the $450 million contract shatters the previous record for a pitcher, which is Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million contract with the Dodgers, Skubal's most recent team. The $50 million average annual salary also shatters the previous record for a pitcher. That was $43.3 million for Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander during their time with the Mets.

Here now are our winners and losers from Skubal's monster contract with the Mets.

According to recent reports, let's start with the obvious: Skubal's a winner because he signed a massive, record-shattering contract. Sign a record deal and you're always a winner in my book. The Mets are a winner because they landed not just the best free agent on the market, but one of the game's best pitchers. Skubal is a power player who can swing a postseason race or a postseason series all by himself. There are very few players like that in the game and now the Mets have one to lead their rotation.

According to recent reports, boras, Skubal's agent, tends to shatter records, not beat them by just a little bit. Alex Rodriguez's contract with the Rangers is his Mona Lisa: A-Rod's $252 million contract was exactly double the largest contract in the four major North American sports leagues at the time (Kevin Garnett's $126 million deal with the Minnesota Timberwolves). Boras did it again with Skubal. He obliterated Yamamoto's total guarantee record, Scherzer's and Verlander's shared average annual value record, and also Max Fried's record deal for a lefty ($218 million). Once again, Boras won significant.

It has been revealed that we can add the Padres here too since they were one of the four teams to meet with Skubal in person this past week, though it was always hard to see San Diego beating out the Blue Jays, Dodgers, and Mets. The Dodgers reportedly held the line at a short-term, high-dollar contract similar to Kyle Tucker's deal, which put them at a disadvantage. Still, they no longer have Skubal in their rotation, and he's irreplaceable. The Blue Jays have been trying to sign top free agents for years (Tucker, Shohei Ohtani, Juan Soto, etc.) and have yet to land the plane. Point is, these teams met and pursued Skubal, then he signed elsewhere. Ergo, losers.

Recent findings suggest that with Skubal off the board, the market for second- and third-tier free agent starters should swiftly pick up. That group includes Michael King, Freddy Peralta, and Trevor Rogers. Skubal signing this early is a substantial win for everyone, really, and especially the other free agent starters. They have more than a week to negotiate and sign before the owners are expected to lock out the players after the current CBA expires at 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 1. Pitchers are coming off the board fast and furious right now. Expect that to continue for another week or so.

To be sure, the Mets' president of baseball operations is a winner because his team now employs Skubal. This is 100% a Steve Cohen contract, though. Stearns has been against long-term contracts for pitchers throughout his career as an executive, even if he mentioned during the GM Meetings that he works on a "case-by-case basis," and it's hard to believe he'd give a pitcher with three elbow surgeries on his resume this contract. It seems likely Cohen was the one pushing this deal across the finish line, and hey, he's the owner; he can do whatever he wants. Stearns is very much against long-term deals for pitchers, though. I imagine he feels at least a wee bit nervous. Plus, he really can't afford another disaster season like 2026.

Recent findings suggest that once again, the top free agent went with a significant market team. The Mets are signing Skubal this offseason. The Dodgers signed Tucker last offseason. The Mets signed Soto the offseason before that. The Dodgers signed Ohtani the offseason before that. The folks who insist baseball needs a salary cap, both the owners themselves and the fans who lean that way, now have more ammunition for their fight. Settle in. It is very, very likely we're in for months of salary cap debate during an extended lockout. That was true even before Skubal signed.

#164841. Kyrie Irving to the Jazz? Why Utah's reported interest in the star Mavericks guard makes no sense

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1440 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

Kyrie Irving to the Jazz? Why Utah's reported interest in the star Mavericks guard makes no sense

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1440 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • They will consider almost any path to improving their rosters, no matter how obscure or unexpected.
  • In a recent development, on Thursday, one such rumor arrived as SNY's Ian Begley reported that the Utah Jazz have given Kyrie Irving "internal consideration as a potential trade candidate." Now, this is common.
  • According to recent reports, so, let's consider this rumor in earnest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NBA teams are remarkably diligent. They will consider almost any path to improving their rosters, no matter how obscure or unexpected. Still, every now and then, a truly bizarre nugget hits the rumor mill and forces us to consider what exactly a team is thinking.

In a recent development, on Thursday, one such rumor arrived as SNY's Ian Begley reported that the Utah Jazz have given Kyrie Irving "internal consideration as a potential trade candidate." Now, this is common. Teams will do due diligence on a wide variety of players leading up to transaction periods in order to make sure they've covered their bases, and Begley gives no indication that there have even been talks between the Jazz and the Dallas Mavericks. Still, as he notes, "you're not gonna spend a lot of time on a player if you don't have any interest in him, so the idea of Utah spending some time internally on Kyrie Irving was interesting.".

According to recent reports, so, let's consider this rumor in earnest. The Jazz entered this season with playoff expectations after four straight years in the lottery. They are 3-13 due to a combination of injuries, players adjusting to a fresh roster and simply poor performance. Utah has shown a willingness to trade for players outside of its perceived timeline before. The Jazz looked at then-33-year-old Jrue Holiday early in their rebuild in 2023, for instance, but backed off when Holiday's camp reportedly made it clear he would not be interested in extending.

Irving, still a star-caliber scorer, has the Mavericks at 8-7 through 15 games. He's averaging over 22 points on roughly his standard efficiency for a Dallas team with pretty limited shooting around him. We can't say at this stage whether or not the Mavericks are willing to trade him. The notion that they might depends on the team's asset deficit (Dallas does not control its own first-round pick again until 2031) and the 15-year age gap between Irving and franchise player Cooper Flagg, but Dallas could easily elect to simply build off this early success.

Sources indicate that if they do take the long view and consider trade offers, Irving could absolutely help a team trying to win right now. Plenty of teams potentially looking for individual shot-creation, like the Detroit Pistons, Houston Rockets and Miami Heat, could be planning pursuits of the future Hall of Famer.

It has been revealed that the question here is why the Jazz, specifically, would be interested in Irving, because on paper, there is perhaps not a single, high-profile player who makes less sense for this roster than he does. Utah's young core revolves around three perimeter players: Keyonte George, Darryn Peterson and Ace Bailey. The Jazz are so strong on that front that Bailey came off the bench to start the season, and it's unclear how exactly they plan to handle their starting five when Lauri Markkanen and Jaren Jackson Jr. return from injuries. If Utah isn't comfortable with Jackson playing center full time, and the Memphis Grizzlies certainly weren't, then one of those five players either needs to get traded or come off the bench.

Industry observers note that adding Irving to this logjam doesn't make sense. Neither does trading one of those players for Irving. George is 23. Bailey is 20. Peterson is 19. Teams that are 10 games below .500 simply don't trade foundational pieces for players a decade or more their senior. They gave up three first-round picks for Jackson largely to improve their defense, and now that Walker Kessler plays for the Los Angeles Lakers, his presence matters more than ever.

Markkanen is the obvious trade candidate of the group, but he's still five years younger than Irving and plays a less saturated position. If Utah viewed Markkanen's max contract as a negative it needed to escape, that would be one thing, but there's just no evidence at this stage that this is the case. They have rebuffed trade interest in Markkanen at every turn. If Dallas were willing to put substantial draft equity on the table to cover the age and positional gaps here, there could perhaps be a conversation, but Dallas isn't in a position to do so.

Recent findings suggest that there's some merit to the idea that Utah might eventually want to shake up its backcourt. There were rumors during the draft process that Peterson's representatives were skeptical of Utah as a landing spot because they also represent George and felt that two score-first guards would clash. Even if the Jazz were prepared to split them up less than 20 games into Peterson's career, Irving himself has typically fared far better when he has been paired with a high-level passer. He won his championship with LeBron James. He's thriving next to Cooper Flagg now. His best trait is, and always has been, his scoring.

According to recent reports, and then, of course, there is the history shared between Irving and Utah's top executive. The CEO of the Jazz is Danny Ainge, who once traded for Irving when he ran the Boston Celtics. Before his second season in Boston, Irving publicly shared plans to re-sign with the Celtics as a free agent in 2019. When the time came, he instead joined the Brooklyn Nets, a divisional opponent. This is the NBA. If LeBron James can reunite with Dan Gilbert, any player-executive reunion is theoretically possible. Nonetheless, Ainge and Irving would seemingly be among the unlikeliest pairings in all of basketball. Put all of this together and this is a puzzling rumor to say the least.

Sometimes a rumor indicates more about a team's significant-picture plans than it does a specific target. For a variety of reasons, some of which we've covered, it seems exceedingly unlikely that the Jazz are going to trade for Irving. However, they've invested the time in considering it, as Begley noted. That means something, even if it doesn't mean a trade is coming.

It has been revealed that the simplest read on this is that Utah is concerned enough about its short-term prospects that it is considering investing in win-now help despite its 3-13 start. That, in itself, makes sense. The Jazz don't control their own first-round pick this season. They have no incentive to lose, and while making the postseason despite starting the season 10 games under .500 is improbable, it just happened a year ago when the 4-14 Charlotte Hornets recovered swiftly enough to reach the Play-In Tournament. The Jazz are 5.5 games out of the No. 10 seed in the Western Conference right now. If they get healthy in time and make the right addition, perhaps they could still make a real run at it.

Skepticism about the George-Peterson fit, for now, should be on the back burner. Though the two fared far better early on when they played separately, both, at least for now, have better net ratings and true shooting percentages in the minutes they've shared than the minutes they haven't. George's usage skyrockets when he plays without Peterson, but that's to be expected with Markkanen and Jackson out.

There may have been concern early in the season, and that might have been when Irving crossed Utah's mind. There may still be concerns down the line when the Jazz have had a longer sample size to evaluate the pairing with the rest of their roster. For now, though, it's simply too early to consider splitting up such a talented tandem, especially right as the team has actually started winning some games.

Sources indicate that however, ball-handling behind them is a valid concern. Utah declined its fourth-year option on backup point guard and former first-round pick Isaiah Collier, and the offense has been 6.5 points per 100 possessions worse with him on the floor this season. Adding a veteran backup point guard, if only to ease Peterson's burden during the minutes George rests, would be sensible. Irving is obviously no backup, but as perhaps the most notable point guard theoretically on the market, it makes sense that the Jazz would at least broach the concept internally.

It has been revealed that ainge hasn't earned the nickname "Trader Danny" for nothing. His teams are almost always at the center of the trade market, and as last year's Jackson deal proved, he's as capable of a stunner as he's ever been. Irving would certainly qualify as one. We shouldn't expect it. It wouldn't really make sense based on what we know now. But in the post-Luka Dončić trade NBA, it would be hard to dismiss basically any rumor involving a player of this stature.
